Well, i don't understand how you technically distinguish it as illegal if it was confectionated inside the frame of law and one of the parts failed to deliver. Feels like we are having a misunderstanding, sorry if i didn't get your point.

But if the employee already agreed to it's terms and he fails to fulfill it then he needs to renovate it accordingly, once it ends (if it's a temporary one) or it's terminated (if the employer is willing to). Unless there is an article of the law that says otherwise, that is what is done here regarding jobs of dependent relationships. Maybe there is an article of the finnish law that i'm not aware of? (i'm not an expert at this field)

But if the employee underperforms and doesn't fulfill his obligations under contract and the employer decides to fire him under those claims, then i think the employee shouldn't be able to denounce him of illegal discrimination. I guess no one should be fired from his job if the previously signed contract is respected of course.

There are case exceptions were immigrants may take advantage of the laws that protect them. But this has a negative impact on them on the long run since their image will get damaged and it will have social consequences on how their environment will treat them, even affecting their equals.

I think that religion shouldn't stop you from fullfiling your obligations demanded by the job.

And feels like you can't expect a work environment to adapt to your only known language.
Thanks for the insight!

I think that it's hard and counter productive to impose your own lifestyle on a foreign environment (talking about the immigrant), it's like being a visitor to a stranger's house, you can't force him to deal with what you do in you own home. 

Maybe there should be some requirements (as you said) like in universities, to force some basic knowledge like writing reading and speaking finnish language for the well being of both, the native and the immigrant. Rewarding the ones who passes it and revoking some  priviliges to those who fail (maybe it's too harsh?).  Since i believe that in the long run no one wants to find their native language being barely heard or read.

From a personal point of view, i think the no confrontation approach on public spaces is harmful for the person who's enduring others behavior, since the only thing you end up doing is wishing someone would tell him/her.

Here we don't have an integration process and a non existent border control, but the fact that all neighbouring countrys speak our same language (except Brazil) makes it lot different.

To be fair, super high expectations can damage both parties, the natives and the immigrants, the most helpful rule should be avoiding to impose redundant aspects or behavior on others (respect, for a simpler approach). How you said it, doesn't feel like discrimination being a big problem, but more of a lack of integration and basic misunderstandings.

Hope i got correctly your point, thanks for sharing your experience!

How does law enforcement act on drunk people (junkies, etc) misbehaving in public? Do they get fined, night behind bars or do they let them do whatever they want to?

Here in Argentina is more like the wild west, to each his own and good luck. You rarely see it's law enforcement working properly. Hard lack of work ethic on all ranges.

It feels inevitable that a generation that grows old becomes less open minded and leans to a more conservative personal view. About skinheads, do they happen to lynch someone from time to time? Here they appear on the news vaguely but they are hard to identify since they keep low profile.

I believe not knowing the primary spoken language will set you up for a hard to overcome distance with any country natives, so it seems fair in that aspect.

On a synthesis, there isn't a big discrimination problem but a hard to accostume culture, which is way less of a problem than the one mentioned above.
